item.title: Breathing & Relaxation Are Important to Our Health
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified fitness instructor for older adults

We do it every day, seven days a week: We breathe. We rarely even think about it, yet, like every other part of our body, our lungs require care as well as exercise.

While breathing in, we take in oxygen; while breathing out, we eliminate carbon dioxide and water. With the help of the heart, this process — a complex one which will not be described here — delivers oxygen to the body. Many people don’t realize that the build-up of carbon dioxide — even more than the lack of oxygen — is what causes us to take a breath.

Responding to our body’s needs at any given moment, the brain regulates the rate and depth of breathing so that the right amount of oxygen is delivered to the muscles and organs. During rest, carbon dioxide levels — and therefore breathing rates — are lower. By contrast, carbon dioxide levels in the blood increase during exercise, and so breathing rates go up.

Breathing rates vary from person to person. The average respiratory rate reported in a healthy adult at rest is usually given as 12 breaths per minute. Sometimes, at the end of fitness class, I ask you to listen to your breathing. Chances are, it’s a bit higher right after exercise and will slow down as you relax.

According to Wikipedia, average respiratory rates per minute by age are:

  • Newborns: 44 breaths
  • Infants: 20–40 breaths
  • Preschool children: 20–30 breaths
  • Older children: 16–25 breaths
  • Adults: 12–20 breaths
  • Adults during strenuous exercise: 35–45 breaths
  • Athletes’ peak: 60–70 breaths

The aging process may reduce oxygen blood levels by as much as 20%. Without good breathing, stale air gets stuck in the tissues of the lungs and prevents fresh oxygen from reaching the bloodstream. Side effects of poor breathing can include overall fatigue, mental “fuzziness”, poor posture, sore rib cage and/or sore muscles.

Within limits, breathing can be controlled consciously, but most of the time the system works on its own. Conscious control of breathing occurs in meditation or during exercise, or in speech or vocal training.

★ ★ ★

Here are four suggestions to keep your lungs strong:

  1. Stop smoking: Get help through your doctor or a stop-smoking program.
  2. Get your annual flu shot: It will protect you from developing potentially deadly complications from respiratory infections.
  3. Exercise: This improves lung capacity and gets more oxygen to your brain.
  4. Eat right and drink plenty of fluids: Proper nutrition and hydration are important, not only for the lungs, but for all of our body’s systems.
★ ★ ★

Breathing exercises can help keep the lungs fit. We do some of these exercises in both Light Fit and Adapted Fit, and you can find many others on the internet.

When we are anxious or tense, we tend to breathe shallow and high. Abdominal breathing — which means to breathe fully from the bottom of your lungs — is considered one of the best breathing exercises of all. It is good for relaxation, release of tension, and anxiety control.

Breathing in (left) and breathing out (right). Thanks to OpenStax, Anatomy & Physiology, for the image (CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

To practice abdominal breathing, follow these steps:

  • Place both hands on your abdomen.
  • Inhale through your nose slowly and deeply. Imagine the air filling up the bottom of your lungs first and then slowly rising to the top. As your lungs fill up with air, they will push the diaphragm down, which pushes the internal organs to the side, allowing your stomach to rise. You should see your hands rise, but your chest should move only slightly. (Count to 6.)
  • Pause for a moment. (Count to 8.)
  • Exhale through your mouth, pursing your lips to make it come out slowly and evenly. (Count to 12.) Note: It should take twice as long to exhale as to inhale.
  • Repeat the entire process 2-3 times daily.
★ ★ ★

In fitness class, I tell you to BREATHE. Don’t hold your breath at any time during exercise. Technically, there is a right and a wrong way to breathe while weightlifting, but HOW you breathe is LESS important than the simple fact that you BREATHE.

If you wish to have a pattern to your breathing while lifting weights, there is a simple rule to follow: Since it’s harder to lift a weight than it is to lower it, you need to synchronize the breathing with the difficulty of the movement: Inhale when the weight is being lowered and exhale when the weight is being raised.

There are two ways to achieve this: (1) Begin at the beginning of the exercise, inhale, then exhale as you exert yourself with the upward or harder movement, or (2) Move to the top of the exercise, inhale as you come down, and exhale as you push back up. If you find this uncomfortable, don’t worry about it. Remember what has already been said: How you breathe is less important than the simple fact that you breathe.

item.title: Brain Exercises: A Few Ideas
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-Certified Fitness Instructor

We know that if we exercise the brain, we may decrease the chances of getting Alzheimer’s or dementia by encouraging new nerve cell growth and increasing communication between nerve cells. Some studies suggest that these activities will continue to stimulate the brain for up to five years.

Below are some ways you can exercise your brain (in addition to attending fitness class). There are many possibilities; these are just a few. The goal is simple: challenge the brain to do something different. If you already do them, great! If you find something new on the list and it intrigues you, feel free to give it a try.

New Skills

🚶 Physical

  • Try a new physical activity: golf, lawn bowling, swimming, tai chi, dancing, yoga, badminton — to name just a few.
  • Challenge your non-dominant hand or foot: Eat or write with the non-dominant hand; shift your weight to the non-dominant foot while at the kitchen sink.

🃏 Mental

  • Learn to read music and/or play an instrument (if you played an instrument in your youth, play it again).
  • Play card games or purchase apps on your phone to play.
  • Learn a foreign language.
  • Learn to use new technology: computers and accessories, phones, video games.

🧠 Brain Games

  • Do crossword or Sudoku puzzles.
  • Try math problems or brain teasers.
  • Memorize a list worth remembering (e.g. Canadian provinces).
  • Memorize poetry, literary passages, or famous sayings that you enjoy.
  • Don’t look at your shopping list but, before you buy, check it.

📖 Reading and Writing

  • Read out loud (to your spouse, your grandchildren, or your friends).
  • Read magazines, newspapers, novels, non-fiction — whatever you enjoy.
  • Keep a diary of your daily activities.
  • Write your own poetry or prose.

🛌 Healthy Habits

  • Exercise (at least 30 minutes 5 times per week).
  • Build muscles (moderate levels 2-3 times a week).
  • Eat a brain-healthy diet. (Include nuts, whole grains, and fresh produce. Avoid trans fats, but enjoy a glass of red wine and a dark chocolate square occasionally.)
  • Establish a regular sleep schedule. (Note: If you have specific problems with insomnia, you may need to see your doctor.)
  • Do breathing exercises or meditate regularly.
  • Each time you shop, take a different route.

item.title: Balancing & Breathing Exercises You Can Do at Home
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-Certified Fitness Instructor, Specialist in Third Age and Special Populations

Choose from the following for a 10-Minute Balancing Practice Session

  1. Foot Circles: Point your foot forward, to the side, and to the back, then raise the foot slightly over the floor and circle it in one direction 4 times, then do the other direction. Repeat on the other foot.

  2. Heel-to-Toe Stand: Stand with the toe of one foot touching the heel of the other foot. Close eyes. Balance. Repeat with the other foot in front.

  3. Heel-to-Toe Walk: Walk 4-5 steps with a heel-to-toe position. Try doing it while moving the head side to side. Try doing it while your eyes are closed.

  4. Instep-to-Toe Walk: Do the same thing as in the Heel-to-Toe Walk.

  5. Baby Steps Walk: Do the same thing as in the Heel-to-Toe Walk.

  6. Stand on One Leg: Lift one leg as far as a bent knee of 90°. Hold. Repeat on the other leg.


Choose from the following for a 10-Minute Breathing Activity

  1. Abdominal Breathing: Place one hand on chest and the other on abdomen. Breathe in slowly and let abdomen rise. Exhale slowly. Watch abdomen sink.

  2. 4-7-8 Breathing: Inhale for 4 counts. Hold for 7. Exhale for 8.

  3. Bellows Breathing: Breathe in and out; three in one second. Produce quick movement of diaphragm, suggesting bellows. Breathe normally after each cycle. Do not do more than 15 cycles. (Tends to make you dizzy.)

  4. Calm Breathing: Inhale to 5 counts. Hold breath to 5 counts. Exhale to 5 counts. Take 3 normal breaths. Repeat 3 times, or for up to 5 minutes.

  5. Chinese Breath: First short inhale, lift arms straight out in front. Second short inhale, lift arms straight out to sides. Third short inhale, lift arms straight over head. Exhale, arms back down to sides.

  6. Humming Breath: Inhale, fill belly. Fill chest. As you exhale, make a humming sound. Relax.

  7. Progressive Muscle Relaxation: Tense a group of muscles for 7-10 seconds. Release. Go limp. Repeat with another group of muscles.

item.title: Learning Styles
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, Group Fitness Instructor

There are 4 predominant learning styles: Visual, Auditory, Read/Write, and Kinaesthetic. While most of us may have some general idea about how we learn best, often it comes as a surprise when we discover what our predominant learning style is. And we can also have a little of each, depending on what it is we are trying to learn.

Visual Learners

Visual learners learn through seeing, so tools like diagrams, flowcharts, pictures and symbols can be key to understanding new concepts.

As University style lectures tend to neglect visual components, it may be difficult for visual learners to stay focused during a long lecture. When taking notes in class, something to try is developing a system of symbols to replace the written word. For example, instead of writing out “female” each time in your notes, simply use the standard symbol. Or instead of writing that the results of a particular test were positive, insert a smiley face!

For visual learners, it is often far easier for recall to work with images as opposed to working with words, as you will picture the image in your head while recalling it—far more difficult when trying to recall the word itself!

Other tricks to try for visual learners include spatially rearranging your page—instead of writing across a page horizontally, write in a way that is more descriptive of the relationship being described—for example, write the words out in a circular pattern if that more truly represents the relationship you are describing. Also, it can be useful to colour code your notes, to create more visual stimulation.

Visual learners should focus on the following:

  • Use graphs, charts, illustrations, or other visual aids.
  • Include outlines and handouts for the subject matter.
  • Eliminate potential distractions while reading.
  • Use diagrams to help you understand.
  • Leave white space in handouts for note taking.
  • Use illustrations and presentations that use color.

Auditory Learners

Auditory learners learn through listening. As such, attending lectures, tutorials, and group discussions are absolutely essential for these learners (it’s also essential for the rest of us, being a read/write learner is no reason to skip lecture!).

If you’re an auditory learner, focus on text book readings by reading them out loud, so you can hear how the words sound. It can also be really helpful to engage in group discussions about course concepts and topics—create a weekly study group to get together weekly just to talk about the things being discussed in lectures.

Leave lots of extra room on your page when taking notes in lectures, and then return to these notes after you’ve had a chance to discuss the material in further detail—supplement with the new information you have.

Auditory learners should try the following:

  • Begin new material with an understanding of what is coming.
  • Conclude with a summary of what was learned.
  • Try to verbalize the question.
  • Read aloud.

Read/Write Learners

Read/write learners learn through—what else?—reading and writing. As such, university style courses suit these types of learners fairly well—plenty of text books and study notes to read.

If you’re a read/write learner, pay special attention to text book glossaries—better yet, make your own as you progress through a course. After lecture, return to your notes for review, read them over, and then create a new, condensed set of study notes. Lists can also be a very useful tool.

And a good tip for all students is to rewrite explanation and notes out into your own words. If you can’t rewrite a definition or describe a concept in your own words, concisely, there is a good chance that there is an aspect of that concept that you don’t fully understand. Return to this concept for further review.

Kinaesthetic Learners

Kinaesthetic Learners learn through doing. This is perhaps the most challenging learning style for university students, as there are not always many opportunities to engage in hands on learning in lectures. For this reason, labs and tutorials become even more essential for these learners.

While studying, try to incorporate all of your senses into the experience—the more of this you can do, the higher your recall will be, as you’ll have multiple cues.

One way to create more useful study notes if you’re a kinaesthetic learner is to fill your notes with several examples for each concept. Try taking an example from the text, or lecture, or lab, and then try creating your own example. As a general rule, the more personal your created example is, the better your recall will be for that example—and hopefully for the concept it is describing! Also try to make as much use of practise questions and exams as possible.

Kinesthetic Learners should consider these techniques:

  • Use activities that will allow you to move.
  • Play music during activities.
  • Use highlighters and colored pencils.
  • Take frequent stretch breaks.
  • Hold on to something to keep your hands busy.
  • Find tasks that involve manipulating materials.

This article draws on ideas from a number of websites; for instance, Wilfrid Laurier University has an excellent site about learning styles. As well, I taught school for 32 years, and my own experience is also a source for the article.

item.title: Health Issues Faced by the Older Adult
item.description:
by Susan Ingraham, Group Fitness Instructor

Four health conditions that many older adults often face are:

  1. hearing loss and tinnitus;
  2. cataracts;
  3. depression; and,
  4. dementia.

This article will do a brief review of all four conditions.

Hearing Loss and Tinnitus

These two things — hearing loss and tinnitus — can occur together or separately. Hearing loss — caused by such things as aging or exposure to loud noises — is strongly linked with tinnitus, but some people with hearing loss never develop tinnitus.

Age-related hearing loss is known as presbycusis; it is progressive, occurs in both ears in roughly equal amounts, and affects the high frequencies first. It is the most common cause of hearing loss worldwide and is estimated to affect approximately two-thirds of people aged 70 or older.

The causes of presbycusis are numerous but generally are a result of at least one of four factors:

  1. Continuous exposure to loud noises (such as music or work related noise);
  2. loss of hair cells (sensory receptors in the inner ear);
  3. inherited factors; and,
  4. aging.

There are different types of presbycusis and the type someone has depends on the specific damage that has been done to the inner ear. Two of the most common types are:

  1. Sensory presbycusis: This hearing loss happens when you lose outer hair cells in the organ of Corti at the base of your cochlea.

  2. Neural presbycusis: Your ability to hear relies in part on nerve cells in your cochlea and the auditory pathway to your brain. You lose nerve cells over time as a part of growing older.

Tinnitus (pronounced tih-NITE-us or TIN-uh-tus) is the perception of sound that does not have an external source, so other people cannot hear it.

Tinnitus is commonly described as a ringing sound, but some people hear other types of sounds, such as roaring or buzzing. It is more common than many people realize — surveys estimate that 10% to 25% of adults have it while children can also have it. For children and adults, tinnitus may improve or even go away over time, but in some cases, it worsens with time. When tinnitus lasts for three months or longer, it is considered chronic.

The causes of tinnitus are unclear, but most people who have it have some degree of hearing loss. Tinnitus is only rarely associated with a serious medical problem. However, some people find that it affects their mood and their ability to sleep or concentrate. In severe cases, tinnitus can lead to anxiety or depression.

Currently, there is no cure for tinnitus, but there are ways to reduce symptoms. Common approaches include the use of sound therapy devices (including hearing aids), behavioral therapies, and medications.

Cataracts

A cataract is a cloudy area in the lens of the eye (the clear part of the eye that helps to focus light). They are very common as a person ages. In fact, more than half of all people age 80 or older either have cataracts or have had surgery to get rid of cataracts.

Most cataracts develop when aging or injury changes the tissue that makes up the eye's lens. Proteins and fibres in the lens begin to break down. This causes vision to become hazy or cloudy. Some genetic disorders that cause other health problems can also increase the risk of getting cataracts.

Cataracts can be removed only with surgery. If your cataract symptoms are not bothering you, surgery is not necessary. You should consider surgery when cataracts keep you from doing things you want or need to do.

Depression

Depression is a mood disorder that causes a persistent feeling of sadness and loss of interest. It affects how you feel, think and behave and can lead to a variety of emotional and physical problems.

Why are seniors at risk of depression? Here are some of the reasons:

  1. Loneliness: Many seniors live alone and have limited means to socialize. They often miss the people with whom they once shared experiences and regular conversations — spouses, friends, neighbours, medical providers, and work colleagues. As a result, they are highly susceptible to feelings of loneliness and isolation.

  2. Immobility: Whether because of physical limitations or transportation constraints, or both, many seniors are not as able to do as much or get around as well as they once did. The loss of a driver’s license is particularly frustrating to some older adults, even while others choose to stop driving.

  3. Lack of Independence: As we age, we are naturally less able to do for ourselves. Declining physical health, unstable balance, falls, memory loss, dementia, impaired mobility, frailty — all these factors contribute to a greater reliance on others. Many seniors struggle with their loss of independence and feel helpless and guilty for asking for help from others.

  4. Lack of Purpose: With aging, some things change — retirement, “empty nest”, failing memory — and those changes contribute to a sense of insignificance among the elderly. Add ageism to that and it’s easy to understand why some seniors become despondent.

  5. Fear of the Future: Even the healthiest seniors know that they’ve lived many more years than they have left. The future may bring physical or cognitive decline, financial threats, changing living arrangements, decreased security, death of self or loved ones, and being a burden upon others. These can lead to anxiety and depression.

There are many ways that an older person can fight these aging issues, but the easiest way is to just get involved: volunteer, take a course, go to fitness class, help a friend.

Dementia

Dementia is a term that is used to cover a variety of symptoms associated with declining mental ability. It is a medical condition of the brain and not specifically a psychological or mental illness, although there can be behavioural and psychological symptoms associated with it.

Dementia symptoms are often overlooked because they are simply thought to be signs of normal aging in older adults. However, dementia is not a natural part of aging and its symptoms include:

  • Forgetfulness
  • Memory loss
  • Reduced reasoning
  • Trouble paying attention
  • Impaired judgment and problem solving
  • Visual perception issues that aren’t related to normal age-related changes
  • Changes in personality and behaviour
  • Any other changes that interfere with a person’s normal daily functions

Dementia is a term used to cover symptoms of mental decline, but there are actually many different types of dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease.

While normal aging can affect cognitive and memory performance, dementia—and therefore Alzheimer’s—is not a part of the normal aging process. Here are examples of normal memory loss for older adults:

  • Misplacing car keys every now and then
  • Forgetting very recent events
  • Having trouble finding a word, but then remembering it later
  • Forgetting the name of an acquaintance

These instances are expected as older adults age. However, it’s important to monitor yourself and/or friends or loved ones to see if these issues continue, increase in frequency, or worsen. If they do, you should seek help from a medical professional to determine if they have dementia or Alzheimer’s disease.

item.title: Aging and Activity
item.description:
What Happens As We Age?

Most of us notice a decline in our body’s ability to move and be active by the age of 30. But, some studies suggest that “participating in regular physical activity can delay the normal aging process by 10 to 20 years.”

Let’s take a look at some of those changes and what types of exercise may help:

  • Cardiovascular and Respiratory Function: Your body’s ability to take in oxygen and transfer it to blood and muscles is known as aerobic capacity; loss of it may tax the heart and lungs, making it harder for you to breathe. Aging and/or disease play a role, but cardiovascular exercise helps maintain aerobic capacity.

  • Muscle Weakness and Loss of Muscle Mass: As our muscles weaken, there are losses in aerobic capacity, bone density, insulin sensitivity, and metabolic rate; it will contribute to increases in body fat, blood pressure, and incidences of cardiovascular disease and diabetes. To counteract the normal loss of muscle mass, older adults will find endurance and resistance training beneficial.

  • Joint Mobility: The ligaments, tendons, muscles, fascia and skin around the joint get stiff and/or shorten as we age, and joint movement can decline 20-50% between 30 and 70. Flexibility can be maintained by safely moving the joints through their full range of motion — but once range of motion is lost, it is difficult to regain.

  • Loss of Bone Mass: Loss of bone mass is a normal part of aging. Fractures are more likely, particularly in the spine, hip and wrist. Studies suggest that exercise helps if it is long-term and involves stressing the skeleton (walking, jogging, stair climbing or squats). For the upper body, resistance training is important.

  • Neurological Function: A lessening of cognitive skills, memory loss, detriments in vision and hearing, loss of motor speed, and balance and gait impairments — all occur as we age. Physical activity has many beneficial effects on memory and cognition, especially if one is challenged to do a variety of tasks at once. There is also evidence that exercise can improve blood supply to the brain, thus stimulating neuronal growth.

Neuroscientists Tell Us What We Can Do

Research reveals that “the best way to forestall or even reverse age-related mental decline is with a regular program of exercise.” They add that “people who exercise regularly can resist this decline.”

Here’s some quotes from the experts:

  1. Dr. Art Kramer, a neuroscientist and director of the Beckman Institute at the University of Illinois, conducted studies that show that even sedentary older adults who begin “regular aerobic exercise programs” can improve cognitive function by 15-20%.

  2. Dr. Brian Christie, another neuroscientist, who teaches at both UBC and UVic, suggests that “the brain is a very demanding organ, requiring vast amounts of nutrients and oxygen.” If we reduce fitness as we age, we “may deprive the brain of the resources it needs to perform well....Exercise [may] actually stimulate growth in the brain.”

  3. Dr. Laura Baker, a neuropsychologist with the Veterans Administration and the University of Washington in Seattle, says there is evidence that “exercise produces growth factors in the brain that preserve and protect neurons.” This may even stimulate stem cells to produce new brain cells — possibly “restoring brain tissue that may have atrophied.”

  4. Dr. Jon Ratey, a psychiatrist at Harvard University, says that this stimulation that Dr. Baker refers to is most likely “because stem cells in the brain are stimulated to produce new neurons....Most studies indicate that forty minutes to an hour of moderately intense aerobic exercise...three or four times a week, will help you reap the cognitive rewards.”

More Research About Aging and Exercise

In the end, we should try to do what's best for ourselves. Here are several studies that tell us more:

  1. A study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine reviewed the histories of 24,281 Canadians. It revealed that “The average yearly healthcare costs for the physically inactive were $1214 higher than healthcare costs of the physically active.”

  2. More than 1500 older adults were involved in a six-year study; the average age was 71 years and 18% of them lived alone. The participants were asked every two years about whether they felt isolated or lacked companionship. People who said they were lonely were more likely to report difficulty in: 1) accomplishing daily living tasks; 2) using their upper body, and 3) climbing stairs. Thirty-eight percent of them reported a decline in mobility, and loneliness was associated with an increased risk of death.

  3. The Longevity Genes Project followed the lives of over 500 Eastern European Jews over the age of 95 along with 700 of their descendants. Responding to many questions, these centenarians exhibited a positive attitude toward life, had an ability to express their emotions, did not display neurotic personalities, and exhibited a high level of conscientiousness. One of the researchers said, “[They] considered laughter as an important part of life and had a large social network. They expressed emotions openly rather than bottling them up.”

  4. A study used data from a survey titled Americans’ Changing Lives, as well as mortality statistics for 1986-2005. It revealed that people who had high levels of social engagement were at a lower risk of death compared to those with less social interaction, even after controlling for other predictors of mortality. Finding ways to interact with others is important: from attending fitness class, to playing bridge, to taking a walk with your grandchild.

  5. Professor Steven N. Blair of the Department of Exercise Science and Epidemiology at the Arnold School of Public Health, University of South Carolina, has been involved in research to determine how much regular physical activity improves our health….at any age. His results were published in an edition of the British Journal of Sports Medicine. Professor Blair says: “There is now overwhelming evidence that regular physical activity has important and wide-ranging health benefits. These range from reduced risk of chronic diseases such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers to enhanced function and preservation of function with age.” As well, “there is strong emerging evidence that activity delays cognitive decline and is good for brain health as well as having extensive benefits for the rest of the body.” Blair discovered that those who exercised lived longer and felt better than those who didn’t. He asserts “that the typical physician is 10-50 times more likely to measure cholesterol, blood pressure, and BMI than to measure fitness.” He recommends that an exercise test be a part of any physical exam.

item.title: Arthritis and Exercise, Part 4: Exercise Guidelines and Considerations
item.description:
Why you Should Exercise if you have Arthritis
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified fitness instructor for older adults

If you have any form of arthritis, here are some guidelines to follow when exercising:

  1. Expect fatigue: Fatigue is a side effect of the disease, especially with RA. Find a balance between exercise and rest, as you need both.

  2. Expect some pain: You should respect and expect pain, especially during exercise. Modifications need to be made based on your personal pain tolerance.

  3. Use the 2-Hour Pain Rule: If you experience more than typical joint pain two hours after exercise, it indicates that you have overexerted. You need to adjust your workload the next time you exercise.

  4. Respect your limits: Only you know how you feel. If the exercise is uncomfortable or hurts, you should stop, slow down, change weights, rest — whatever seems right for you. Work at your own pace and don’t attempt to keep up with anyone else.

  5. Warm-ups should be long and slow: The warm-up phase is an essential component of the workout. Your instructor should begin with slow, range-of-motion exercises and gentle large muscle movements.

  6. Use heat prior to exercise: A hot shower, heating pad, electric blanket, or hot towel is sometimes recommended before exercise. Heat helps to decrease pain and stiffness and may make exercise easier.

  7. Progress slowly: Modify whenever necessary. Decrease repetitions and speed of the movement when appropriate.

  8. Use proper body mechanics: Use your joints in their most stable position.

  9. Avoid jarring movements: Avoid quick directional changes as they can compromise joints and aggravate joint pain.

  10. Follow the tenets of joint protection: If you follow the basic tenets of joint protection, your joints will be stabilized and in their strongest, most workable position. The basic tenets of joint protection are: (1) do not compromise the joint; (2) limit extreme weight-bearing flexion (e.g. don’t do a deep squat); (3) use positions that stabilize the joint (e.g. keep wrist in line with the arm); (4) never force joints into uncomfortable positions; (5) use stronger joints for support whenever possible; (6) avoid being in one position for a prolonged period of time; (7) conserve energy; (8) avoid overexertion or overloading of joints; (9) use adaptive equipment when necessary; and (10) stop any movement at the point of pain.

  11. Attempt complete and full range of motion movements, as much as can be tolerated: This might be accomplished by decreasing the speed of the movement, a slower tempo of music, warming up with range of motion activities, and flexibility stretching at the end. Some activities reduce or eliminate stress on the joints, such as swimming and gentle walking.

  12. Use isometric exercises: These exercises use a stable joint position. Pressing the hands together, pressing down on a ball, squeezing the ball — these are isometric exercises, and they reduce joint movement yet strengthen muscles.

  13. Increase chest expansion: Do deep-breathing exercises before and after exercise.

  14. Include Relaxation: Relaxation reduces muscular tension and soothes muscles and joints. Every exercise session should end with flexibility and relaxation.

  15. Avoid becoming chilled: Cold drafts and/or becoming chilled while exercising leads to increased muscle tension. Avoid being in front of the fan or near an open window while exercising.

  16. Use appropriate footwear: Find a shoe that provides plenty of room for your toes, a stable and comfortable sole, extra cushioning and space for orthotics, and possibly velcro for easy closure.

  17. Try to exercise at the best time of day for you: People with RA tend to be less stiff and sore later in the day. Those with OA may be better able to tolerate exercise in the morning before activities of the day have increased their pain.

  18. Use medication properly and talk to your doctor: Follow the schedule your doctor has recommended. Let your doctor know how you are feeling and explain what your exercise regimen entails.

These are all things within your control and, if followed, will help you have some control over your condition. Hopefully, your exercise instructor is well-versed in this information, as well, and will help you to exercise properly.

Source: Exercise and Arthritis by Stephanie Harris, MD, and Gwen Hyatt, MS

item.title: Arthritis and Exercise, Part 3: Exercise Design
item.description:
Why you Should Exercise if you have Arthritis
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified fitness instructor for older adults

We know that regular, moderate physical activity has many benefits. As well, research shows that well-regulated exercise does not produce or aggravate joint symptoms. More specifically, some level of physical activity is necessary to preserve joint function. A combination of aerobic exercise, strength training, stretch and flexibility — taught by a qualified instructor — is the most effective.

The primary goals of an exercise program for those suffering from arthritis are:

  • Restore or maintain joint range of motion: Moving the joints regularly is important to maintain flexibility so that daily activities can be done.

  • Restore or maintain muscle strength: Strengthening exercises can increase tone and functional strength of the muscles surrounding the joint, making it easier to move the joint.

  • Interrupt the Chronic Pain Cycle: When moving the joint is painful, there is a tendency to stop moving it. Continued disuse of the joint may cause stiffness and a shortening of the muscles and connective tissues around the joint (known as joint contracture). Put very simply: loss of movement leads to loss of function.

  • Improve cardiorespiratory endurance: Low-impact aerobic exercise is safe and desirable for individuals with arthritis. Not only does it contribute to one’s overall fitness level, it also will mean less joint stiffness.

  • Improve posture and body awareness: Posture may be improved through balance and coordination exercises.

  • Relieve stiffness: Regular exercise is critical in maintaining ease of movement.

  • Maximize pulmonary function: Breathing and chest expansion exercises encourage maximal lung function.

  • Promote relaxation: Any exercise program requires a relaxation period at the end. Relaxation techniques soothe the muscles and decrease stress.

  • Enhance quality of life: Exercise may improve self-image and self-esteem. Positive social interaction in a class may increase one’s feeling of self-worth and the positive feeling of knowing that you have the ability to take care of yourself.

Source: Exercise and Arthritis by Stephanie Harris, MD, and Gwen Hyatt, MS

item.title: Arthritis and Exercise, Part 2: How to Manage Arthritis
item.description:
Why you Should Exercise if you have Arthritis
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified fitness instructor for older adults

The most common medications used for arthritis are:

  • analgesics for pain reduction
  • anti-inflammatory agents for inflammation reduction
  • immunosuppressants for immune system suppression
  • antidepressants for helping reduce depression and anxiety

Surgical interventions — to relieve pain and improve function — are becoming more common for RA: hip and knee replacements are the most common, but surgery is also done on shoulders, elbows and ankles.

There are other therapies that seem to help some people — from massage to braces to Chinese medicine. Each person must decide what works for them.

In addition to medical intervention and therapies, there are some simple strategies that can be done by everyone — they can help to control pain, improve independence and quality of life, and slow the progression of the disease.

Here are five strategies that may help:

  • Weight reduction: Even modest weight loss (as little as 5 pounds) may be beneficial by putting less stress on the joints and their function.

  • Rest and relaxation: Deep breathing, visual imagery while listening to music, tensing and relaxing individual muscles, and self-generated meditation exercises — all can be done at the end of an exercise class or alone at home in the comfort of your favourite chair.

  • Joint protection: Limiting stress to the joints is important, so remember these basic principles of joint protection: (1) respect pain; (2) distribute the load over stronger joints; (3) avoid sitting or standing for long periods of time; (4) reduce weight; (5) use good posture and body mechanics; (6) use the minimum amount of force necessary; (7) balance work with rest; and, (8) remain active.

  • Energy conservation: Conserving your energy overlaps with protecting your joints. Planning ahead, organizing tasks, and taking regular breaks will help to conserve your energy.

  • Exercise: See Parts 3 and 4 for exercise guidelines and principles.

Source: Exercise and Arthritis by Stephanie Harris, MD, and Gwen Hyatt, MS

item.title: Arthritis and Exercise, Part 1: Overview of Rheumatic Disease
item.description:
Why you Should Exercise if you have Arthritis
by Susan Ingraham, BCRPA-certified fitness instructor for older adults

Most adults have one or two chronic health conditions by the time they reach 60, but many people manage their disease(s) and live normal and productive lives. Physical disuse and disability in people with chronic disease is, however, a major contributor to premature aging. Dr. Waneen Spirduso in her book, Physical Dimensions of Aging, identifies the three things which contribute to the aging process:

  • Dimension #1: Time. This is the normal aging process, which eventually drains energy and vitality.

  • Dimension #2: Disease. Genetic predispositions to diseases, or exposure to external agents, will damage one or more bodily systems and lead to weakness, fatigue, and frailty.

  • Dimension #3: Disuse. Sitting for long periods of time, extended bed rest, or general inactivity dramatically accelerates aging. “A lifetime of physical disuse can have catastrophic effects on strength, cardiovascular function, mobility, and physical as well as mental function.”

We obviously have little control over the first two dimensions: time and disease. But the third one, disuse, is completely within our control. Arthritis and other rheumatic conditions are among the most common chronic diseases, and they often lead to disuse. What is arthritis? There are two common types:

Osteoarthritis (OA) — the most common form of arthritis which worsens over time — is a progressive joint disease. There is a gradual loss of cartilage from the joints and, for some, joint inflammation. The most common symptoms are pain, stiffness and loss of joint motion. It most often affects the hands, knees, hips, and spine.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune inflammatory disease; the immune system turns against the body, attacking the joints. The lining surfaces of the joints become inflamed; it can also affect the surface surrounding the heart and the lungs. It tends to occur on both sides of the body, usually involving multiple joints of the hands and feet, although any joint can be involved.

There are other types of rheumatic disease but they are not as common as OA and RA. These include: spondyloarthropathy, Reiter’s syndrome, gout, psoriatic arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, juvenile arthritis, systemic lupus, scleroderma, and fibromyalgia.

The next section will discuss how to manage arthritis.

Source: Exercise and Arthritis by Stephanie Harris, MD, and Gwen Hyatt, MS

item.title: Book 3: Julia
item.description:
Chapter 11: Connecting with Grace

My mother and I felt that Gracie needed to be in Kansas City as soon as we knew that Sarah Etta had written a will which just didn’t make sense. My beloved older sister was clearly affected by the morphine she took for the pain after her accident. We had to protect her daughter’s rights to her mother’s estate while we also protected our own.

But it was a lot for an 11-year-old child to take in. We had taken her away from the only family she knew — my brother, Samuel; his wife, Martha; and their daughter, Caroline, and son, Fred. She had lived a quiet life in quiet farm areas and her Uncle Samuel suffered from paranoia (he was hospitalized in Kansas City for nearly a decade in the early 20th century), so she had learned to be quiet and not bother the adults in the family.

Both my mother and I were very involved with the trial in order to break the will and we didn’t want to subject Gracie to all that unpleasantness. So, while her lawyer protected her rights during the court trial, we enrolled Gracie in school. She was shy and timid, but she did like to learn and she took to her studies quickly and easily. Even during the trial, though, she was coming home to live with me, eat her meals, and sleep.

The verdict, as reported in the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo, June 2, 1891

After the trial, things got much easier and I had more time to spend with her. Just like Sarah Etta and I had been somewhat overwhelmed by the big city, Gracie was also a little nervous. But, as time went by, and I took her to more and more activities, she opened up a little. It wasn’t in her nature, however, to be talkative and outgoing. Learning that she had no father was difficult for her to accept and the confusion about her middle name being Cuba remained with her. Even my mother and I were not completely sure what Sarah Etta’s motives were, but we knew that she thought it would provide a hint to Gracie about who her father was.

Gracie had spent plenty of time in cold, snowy weather, having lived first in Minnesota and then in South Dakota, before she came to live with Mother and me. There were three storms, two of which were great fun and we built snowmen and walked through the streets where it was so quiet you could have heard a pin drop. There was a big snowstorm in February 1894 when more than 15” fell in two days; another February storm in 1899 was very cold — below 20°F for nearly three days; and nearly a foot of snow fell in one day on 27 February 1900. Gracie and I liked the snow, but we were not crazy about the cold.

I felt that the best way to help Gracie adjust was to keep her busy and to show her that her grandmother and her aunt loved her dearly. I tried to be home when she came home from school; I couldn’t always do that during the trial, but once that was done, I was usually able to leave work at the Alamo Building and come home to take care of Gracie. We would talk about her day and I’d help her with her homework if she needed it (but she rarely needed it).

Every fall, Kansas City held a grand festival. It was spectacular and to a little girl like Gracie it was pretty thrilling. It was based on Greek mythology and every year they had a float carrying the goddess Athena. The floats were pulled by horses or mules and to add to the excitement they were lit by torches. It was quite a sight to see. I took Gracie to several of these parades, but I don’t remember which years.

On May 14, 1893, Fairmount Park opened and Gracie was 13 — just the right age for such a park. It was an amusement park, located out toward the edge of the city (toward Independence, Missouri). We could reach it by train for 15 cents! There was a large lake where you could ride in a boat; there was a dancing pavilion and an electric fountain that was lit up in colours at night. One time I went with her through the Crystal Maze — a mirror maze. We learned that you could get through it easily if you looked down at the floor and followed the boards which led to the next section. There were also balloon ascensions and parachute jumps — but Gracie had no desire to try either of those. Nor did I! The park was open every year and Gracie went to it several times. I don’t remember how many.

As each year passed and Gracie became more comfortable with her new reality, she did open up a little bit. But she never really got over knowing that she was illegitimate and she didn’t want people to know. I had no problem telling people I was her mother, but I’m not sure that she was happy about that. But the reality is that we became very close and she did think of me almost like her mother.

Effie’s monument in New Haven, Connecticut

My sister Effie died on June 25, 1896, and for several days, my mother, Gracie, and I were quiet and still. Effie and her husband had moved to Tucson, hoping that the dry air would help her fight off tuberculosis. But, in the end, she was unable to do that. We didn’t feel that we had the time to go to Tucson for the funeral, but her body was taken to New Haven, Connecticut, for burial because that is where her husband was from. When the body came through Kansas City, we went to view the body and talk to her husband.

A few days after that, I took Gracie to Swope Park. This was a new park that had opened recently (actually it was on the same day that Effie died) and I thought that going to the park would help Gracie to deal with another loss. It was a beautiful park — just lots of places to walk and look at nature. There were trails that wound through woodlands and grassy meadows. Gracie loved it because it was more of what she was used to.

Gracie and I had many conversations about what she might want to do with her life. Mother and I were determined to help her find a skill or trade — something that would allow her to take care of herself. Things were a lot different for women than they had been for Aunt Clarinda, whose troubles had occurred more than 30 years before. At some point, perhaps while she was attending high school, Gracie told me that she liked the idea of becoming a nurse. So we began to make that her goal.

I married James Alan Ham on 5 June 1893, but Gracie continued to live with us, or sometimes at her grandmother’s house, throughout the 1890s. She was busy with school, and then nursing school. Once she got to nursing school, she lived with other student nurses who were in training.

Perhaps one of the biggest thrills that Gracie and I shared was going to Buffalo Bill’s Wild West Show in October of 1896 when Gracie was 17. Such an exciting experience and one I know that my sister, Sarah Etta, would have loved. Most remarkable of all was Annie Oakley, the woman sharpshooter. We loved her!

Gracie always loved to read. She would read for hours and hours. When the new public library opened on September 1, 1897, she was thrilled. We both went to see this beautiful new building. The interior stacks had glass floor panels which allowed natural light to filter down through the stacks. The upper floors housed the Western Gallery of Art; it had historical paintings, sculptures, and art collections. Gracie loved to just go there and sit — it was private and it was quiet.

By the end of the century, Gracie turned 20 and she was involved in going to nursing school. She lived in a dormitory with other nursing students, so I didn’t see her as often, but we got together as often as we could. We still did things together and one I remember well was going to see the Electric Park. It opened in the East Bottoms in June of 1900. There were thousands of electric lights, a coloured fountain with shows every night, and singers. Beer was piped straight from the Heim brewery next door — but by then Gracie was a total teetotaler and would not touch anything alcoholic. Perhaps she realized that her mother drank too much and she didn’t want to become dependent on it; perhaps, as well, her religion told her not to drink. Three years before, she had participated in a speaking contest sponsored by the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union, and her topic was, “What shall we do with the Saloon?” She had won first place and received a gold medal. I learned early not to argue with her on that particular topic.

So from 1890 through to 1910, I helped Gracie as much as I could. We grew close and we loved each other. I was proud of her accomplishments in nursing. She worked hard and did well. I don’t think she was ever comfortable with her birthright, though, and she never admitted to anyone that Sarah Etta was her mother. She did meet a nice young man and they got engaged, but then she decided that she wanted to leave the hustle and bustle of the city and she applied for a job in Caton, New York, to be the nurse to an elderly lady. That job would lead her into new directions. In the meantime, we always stayed in touch.

item.title: Book 3: Julia
item.description:
Chapter 10: Life in Kansas City with Sarah Etta

I was so excited to go with Sarah Etta to Kansas City. She had written letters often when she had been away, and when she came home to have her darling little baby, Gracie, she talked and talked about her life there. After Gracie was born, Sarah Etta stayed with us for a while in order to nurse her. But Sarah Etta knew that she couldn’t stay with Gracie forever. She had to return to Kansas City and make sure her businesses were still running well and making a profit. Mother, Sarah Etta, and I went together to Waseca to leave little Gracie with my oldest brother, Samuel, and his wife, Martha. They had a small daughter, Caroline, and they were willing to take in Gracie. Sarah Etta had plans for Gracie to some day come to Kansas City and learn who her real mother was.

We said good-bye to everyone — Samuel, Martha, Caroline, Gracie, and Mother — and boarded the train for the ride to Kansas City. I was lucky I was going with my sister because she had done all of this already and thus I felt safe and secure when I was with her. Although Sarah Etta was sad to leave Gracie behind with Sam and Martha, she was excited to get back to Kansas City and her businesses. She wanted to teach me a lot of things and I was looking forward to every minute.

My marriage to Bill had not ended, but he was not a well man. He had been living in Kansas City before Sarah Etta and I got there late in 1879. Like Sarah Etta, I took a pseudonym for my work: Daisy Brown. I worked in Sarah Etta’s resorts, both the one on Grand Avenue and the one on Third Street. But, I have to confess that I didn’t enjoy it as much as my sister did and Bill preferred that I find something else to do with my time to earn a living.

So while I was busy working for Sarah Etta, still known as Kitty Brown, I also looked for work as a seamstress (I happen to think I was as good as my sister — perhaps even better). I was also a good stenographer so I began to look for work in that field as well. I liked to keep my life private, so I had fun changing Bill’s name and mine and giving the City Directory people a lot of silly names. I changed Larraman to Lamore and used that as my official name for many years to come. For a few years, however, I was running Sarah Etta’s resort for her on Grand Avenue. Bill and I sometimes got together, but he was busy with his work and I certainly didn’t see him every day. Besides, he didn’t really like what I was doing for a living.

Here are the entries in some of the city directories when I first went to Kansas City. I deliberately made it unclear who I was and what I did for a living, but in nearly all entries there is a certain amount of accuracy.

  • 1883 and 1884: Daisy Brown, living at 125 Grand Avenue (Kitty Brown’s resort)
  • 1888: Julia Lamore, Alamo Building, stenographer
  • 1889: H Jsiorejulia, 1011 Main Street
  • 1890: Julia H. LaMore, 1011 Main Street, stenographer
  • 1891: Jails La More, Occupation: Far Rtniiu
  • 1892: Ji Julia, 918 Woodland
  • 1893: J.H. Lamore, 918 Woodland, draughtsman and dressmaker.
Barnum’s circus parade at 8th and Main, 1886

From 1880 to 1885, Sarah Etta and I enjoyed the sights and sounds of the city. Sometimes I was left breathless by the noise and the bustle, and there were so many activities to go to. Perhaps the best thing we ever attended was Barnum’s circus. They came to Kansas City in October of 1884 and there was a big parade down Main Street when they arrived. P.T. Barnum named his circus the “Greatest Show on Earth” and I have to admit that it was pretty spectacular. I had never seen an elephant before, and they had two as their star attractions: a white elephant — which they said was sacred because he was white — that had come from Burma, and Jumbo, the biggest elephant anyone had ever seen. I could not believe how large Jumbo was. I was a bit concerned about how he was being treated, though. He had been in the London Zoo for many years and given many children a ride, but P.T. Barnum bought him for $10,000 — a truly princely sum. While he drew large crowds everywhere he went, I couldn’t help but think that he might have preferred a bit more privacy. Unfortunately, Jumbo was killed by a train in St. Thomas, Ontario, Canada, the following year. We couldn’t believe it. He was being loaded onto a train with his handler when they were hit by an unscheduled freight train! Such a tragedy!

Sarah Etta and I watched the parade together with a lot of the other girls from the resorts, and Sarah Etta and I got tickets to actually see the show. It was wonderful; we both loved it. Sarah Etta challenged me to ride Jumbo, so we both went together and rode that huge animal. I was nervous, but Sarah Etta laughed the whole time.

Both Sarah Etta and I wanted to educate ourselves. Our childhood educations had not been perfect — and I think I got a better education in Minnesota than Sarah Etta did when we were still in West Turin. But Sarah Etta had a burning desire to read, to learn as much as she could, and I didn’t disagree with that. So, whenever we had the time, we tried to go to events that would improve our knowledge of the world.

One of those events was on Monday, 17 April 1882. We went to listen to Oscar Wilde, the famous Irish writer, talk about “The Decorative Arts.” We weren’t sure just what that would be about but we knew we might learn something if we went and listened. He was speaking at the Coates Opera House which I think I heard seated about 1800 people, but a lot of things were going on in Kansas City at the time and he drew a small crowd, but we were glad we went. Sarah Etta and I got so many great ideas about how to decorate our homes and the resorts. He talked about the philosophy of aestheticism (I had to learn that word) which focused on interior design. He offered real, practical advice on how to decorate your home. He was opposed to mass-produced furniture and objects. Since our father had been a carpenter, we fully understood what he meant, although I am not sure I agreed with his idea that industrial furniture actually damaged people’s souls. I did agree with his comment, though, that industrial furniture could eliminate beauty from every life. Another interesting twist to his talk: The man was quite the dresser. He wore a velvet, cutaway coat, knee breeches, a Byron collar, and a diamond pin. Considering how much Sarah Etta loved clothes, she was very fascinated by this man’s attire. I think we both liked him because he was a bit of a rebel — and so were we.

Another event we really enjoyed was the Inter-State Fair which began in 1882 and lasted until 1887. This event was always held in the fall at some new fairgrounds near Westport. Special trains left downtown every half hour, but you could also get there by horsecar, carriage, and wagon. We thought at first about just going in Sarah Etta’s carriage with Prince, but Sarah Etta became concerned about leaving Prince in a somewhat strange place. So we opted to take one of the trains.

It was a very large area and featured a half-mile racetrack. This was perhaps the best part — especially for Sarah Etta. There were bookmakers and you could bet — which Sarah Etta did — but I was much more likely to just watch. The grandstand was three decks high and had a cupola to cover us if it rained. Of course, there was lots of food and drink, including beer, whiskey, and soda pop, as well as cigars, of course. There were livestock and produce exhibits, but it was the horse racing, pacing, trotting, and Roman-style chariot racing that Sarah Etta truly loved. I think it was 1883 when a pacer named Daisy D won every single race — and my sister had bet on her every time. We went to that fair at least three times before Sarah Etta had her terrible accident in late 1885. (Eventually, the fair was moved to a different site, but that was after Sarah Etta’s accident when, of course, we weren’t going to many activities at all.)

Living in Kansas City meant there was constant change and incredible improvements such as a new newspaper, the Kansas City Evening Star, electric lights used in about a dozen stores on Main Street in 1882, and the first cable cars in June of 1885. Those cable cars were very handy for the steep 9th Street hill from the Union Depot, for instance, although Sarah Etta still preferred to drive up that hill with Prince pulling her. Sadly, she might not have been injured so badly if she had chosen to take a cable car rather than her own carriage with Prince pulling her. The cable cars and horses often had conflicts.

A mule-drawn streetcar on the Kansas City & Westport line, 1870 (Missouri Valley Special Collections, Kansas City Public Library)

At first, there were streetcars pulled by mules, but the new cable car system had no animal in front of it and it could move much faster. It disrupted the city’s horse-and-carriage traffic immensely. It was a major undertaking as they had to lay down a large infrastructure which meant digging deep trenches through major thoroughfares to bury the steam-powered pulleys and cables. The horses’ hooves did not like the car’s mechanism which latched on the moving underground rope. As well, cable cars moved rapidly without an animal in front. There was a loud, continuous mechanical humming of the underground cable which terrified horses, causing frequent runaways, horrendous throws, and street collisions. As well, there are some very steep hills in Kansas City, and these cable cars occasionally broke and sometimes would even come flying down the hill on their own. Those cable cars began operating with regularity by June of 1885 and Sarah Etta had her accident in the fall of that year.

Crowds view the wrecked Jackson County Courthouse, at 2nd and Main, after the tornado of 11 May 1886 (Missouri Valley Special Collections, Kansas City Public Library)

I lived in Kansas City from 1880 to 1927, occasionally living elsewhere but always returning to Kansas City. During that time, there were several tornadoes. I was always able to get to safety, but they could be frightening, especially when you huddled inside and could hear the noise of roofs being ripped off their buildings.

After Sarah Etta’s terrible accident, I nursed her, despite how mean and cruel she became as she attempted to deal with the horrendous pain which would never go away. After her death in early 1890, we all fought the will which she had written while completely out of her mind on morphine because of the pain from the accident. We made sure Gracie had a lawyer so that her rights would be protected.

Then after all of that was resolved, I lost Bill, too, who died unexpectedly in 1892. I concentrated on taking care of Sarah Etta’s daughter, Gracie (more discussion about that in the next chapter).

However, Mother and I both managed to find love and marriage in the 1890s. I married James Alan Ham on 5 June 1893, and we eventually adopted a little boy from Scotland whom we named James Alan Ham, Jr. Mother actually managed to marry before me — 10 November 1892, to John Kell. They lived together happily until Mother died on 29 February 1904.

In June 1896, we also lost my little sister, Effie, who had married well and then became very ill with tuberculosis. When she was told by the doctor she would not live more than another day, she decided to end it herself. While her husband was in the back of the house, she found his revolver and shot herself.1 My mother had suffered some terrible losses but the deaths of Bessie and Effie were the most difficult for her to handle. I stayed close by and tried to get her through it.

Effie’s death, as reported in the Arizona Daily Star, Tucson, June 1896

From the moment Sarah Etta died, I made it my mission to take care of Gracie. To show her the love and affection that I knew Sarah Etta wanted to give her. I had never been a mother before and I didn’t know if I was up to the task, but I was certainly going to try as hard as I could to make Gracie know that she was loved and protected.

Author’s Note: The women in Sisters were real people, and I have told their story as accurately as I can for lives lived in the 19th century. I can prove and support many of the facts with records from the time. But no record can tell me exactly what someone said, and for some events I know only portions of the story. So I have also had to use my imagination, to put you, the reader, inside the head of each woman as she tells her own story.

Chapter 9: My Childhood

I have always felt that my childhood was almost idyllic. That may seem odd, considering what my mother went through while giving birth to eleven children — one more child than even her own mother had given birth to — as well as the nightmare she lived through with her older sister, Clarinda, and the difficulties with my father.

I was born on 20 October 1861, just a year after my Aunt Clarinda met her death at Sing Sing Prison for Women. My mother had already given birth to six children before me: Samuel, Lafayette, Sarah Etta, Leonard, Susan, and Cassius. Before I arrived, Mother had already lost a son, Lafayette, and a daughter, Susan, and she lost Cassius in December 1862, when I was just a baby. After my birth, she had four more babies — all girls — Bessie, Clarria, Effie, and Flora. Clarria and Flora died as infants, while Bessie and Effie would face much more difficult endings.

I was just four years old when my parents decided that we had to leave West Turin and find a new life in another place. I have little memory of West Turin, though by the time we moved I had been out and about with my older sister, Sarah Etta, many times. For me, Sarah Etta was almost my mother. She once told me that she was given the responsibility of taking care of me almost from the time I was born. She certainly taught me about all that the family had endured before I came along, including a great deal of detail about Aunt Clarinda’s story.

Because of these reminders of what had happened to Aunt Clarinda, I knew from an early age that, even though I was a girl, I had a right to live my life the way I wanted to live it. My father, Baker Brand, was not in my life very much. He was a carpenter and he worked for other people, making them furniture or helping them to build a house. He wasn’t around a lot, and Mother never talked about him with any great love or affection. I found him hard to talk to and somewhat distant throughout the time he lived with us before my parents got a divorce. Basically, I think my mother just felt that he didn’t know how to take care of and support a family.

Before we left West Turin, my mother gave birth to my younger sister, Bessie, when I was not quite two years old. We were so near in age that we truly grew up together with a close bond. Because I was the older, I sometimes took on a motherly role with her, but mostly we just played together.

❧   ❧   ❧

I have some memories of the train and boat rides we took to get to Minnesota. Sarah Etta, Bessie and I tended to stick together with Sarah Etta taking on the motherly role with her two younger sisters. It became a “grand adventure” for the three of us.

Clarria was still a baby when we left, and we stopped first in Wisconsin, where my parents had once considered staying. But Clarria died there in October 1865, not long after we arrived, and Mother did not want to remain in Wisconsin, so we moved on to Faribault, Minnesota. Once there, we seemed to settle down a little bit. Mother gave birth to two more girls — Effie Bee and Flora Emma — but Flora only lived for six months. My mother had been 41 years old when Flora was born and after Flora’s death I think she decided that enough was enough.

Therefore, by October of 1872, after the death of little Flora, our family was not going to grow any more. I had two older brothers — Samuel Perkins and Leonard William — and one older sister — Sarah Etta. Younger than me was Effie; we had lost Bessie only two months before.

I looked up to Sarah Etta and we often talked about some day going to a big city and making a lot of money. Sometimes it seemed like that was all my mother and father argued about: money. There was never enough, according to my mother, and my father never seemed to have the spirit to argue with her. He liked doing his carpentry and he was a quiet man, but he didn’t truly support us. Sarah Etta and Mother were always talking about ways that they could make money — and going to a big city to do it was the definite plan. They had watched Grandpa Higby buy and sell land often in West Turin, and it made him pretty wealthy. They thought they might be able to do the same thing. But they had to find a way to make money first in order to buy land.

We lived in Richland in Rice County, Minnesota. I was too young to remember West Turin as well as Sarah Etta could, but Richland became the town that I considered my childhood home. Nearby Faribault was the county seat, and we often went there for shopping and getting other necessities. But it was quiet in Richland and I liked that. Richland is also close to Waseca which is where my oldest brother, Samuel, and his wife, Martha, lived after they were married. Waseca was about 25 miles south of us in Richland, but we didn’t see them often.

❧   ❧   ❧

The saddest and most difficult part of my life in Richland was when my little sister, Bessie, died so suddenly in a tragic accident on the farm. Mother blamed my father for Bessie’s death because he had allowed Bessie to ride a horse in front of the reaper. This happened in August of 1872, and I think it was clearly the moment when my mother decided that she could not tolerate my father any longer. Still, it took another two years to accomplish that.

In 1874, after 26 years of marriage, my parents divorced. This was something that my mother had wanted to do for many years. After Aunt Clarinda’s impossible situation, my mother was determined she would not go down the same path. She bided her time and waited for some of the laws to change — which they did. Aunt Clarinda would not have been able to get a divorce except if her husband had committed adultery, but by 1874 the laws allowed other reasons, and my mother could finally divorce my father. My father immediately left the area after their divorce, and my mother was now free, but Sarah Etta and I knew that she would need help to keep us all fed and dressed.

❧   ❧   ❧

Julia and William’s marriage, from the Minnesota, Marriages Index, 1849–1950 (Ancestry.com)

On 23 January 1876, I got married to William T. Larraman. He was my first love. Although he was older than me by six years, he had been the big brother of a friend of mine, and we loved each other so much that we enjoyed a close relationship and I suddenly found myself pregnant. I was 14 and William was 20. My mother was very upset when she learned I was pregnant but she felt strongly that we should marry so that the child would be legitimate. And so we married. I did love Bill, but I was quite young to have a child and, unfortunately, my little boy died on the same day he was born.

Bill was pretty devastated by the loss of our child, and so he left for a while, trying to find work, but he always came back. By then, my sister, Sarah Etta, had already gone to Kansas City to begin to find a way to earn money for herself and for the family. She wrote letters back to us and I was mesmerized by those letters, telling us about all that she was doing in Kansas City. I wanted to go there, too, and not only work with her, but also see if I could find out what I wanted to do to also earn a living. But before I could do that, Sarah Etta found herself in a difficult predicament, one that she couldn’t fix.

In late 1878, my beautiful and talented sister became pregnant, and unlike my situation she was unable to marry the father of her child. She wrote to Mother and told her what had happened. I know that Mother was angry, but she adored Sarah Etta, so she was prepared to help her in any way that she could. Sarah Etta remained in Kansas City until she could no longer hide her pregnancy. Then she came to live with us. Her little girl, Gracie, was born there with us, and a few weeks later we took the baby down to our older brother’s place in Waseca. Samuel and his wife, Martha, were willing to take in Gracie. They already had one child, Caroline, but Martha welcomed Gracie as her own.

After leaving the baby with Sam and Martha, Sarah Etta and I headed for Kansas City. Sarah Etta was anxious to get back to work and to attend to her financial situation. I wanted to be there to help whenever I could — and also earn money for myself and my family, especially Mother. It was the beginning of a very different life for me. I was a grown-up with major responsibilities and I was ever so excited to go to Kansas City.

Chapter 8: Looking Back

Today, I celebrate my 62nd birthday — 5 February 1893. I don’t know how many years I have left, but it’s been a life full of extremely difficult and emotional lows as well as wonderful highs, especially with my children.

My mother and father — Tryphena Perkins Higby and Abijah Isaac Higby — had a strong influence on me. My mother gave birth ten times to bring me and my siblings into the world. Not all of us survived — Cyrus, just two months old; Clarinda, dying amongst criminals; Norman, just four months old; Salmon, just a year old; James Knox, lost to us when he was only 28 years old; and little Kay, just two years old when she passed.

I was my mother’s 5th child, her second daughter, and I have thus far outlived six of my siblings with only brothers left: Samuel Perkins, Jared Stratton, and Andrew Jackson. My brothers have remained in West Turin, New York, where all of us were born, but after Clarinda’s terrible ordeal, I could no longer live there. My mother, completely crushed by what happened to Clarinda, died just six years after Clarinda — in 1867. My father remarried but he also soon gave in, passing away just four years after my mother — in 1871.

Growing up in West Turin was not all bad and difficult, but my sister and I figured out from a fairly early age that girls were not treated the same as boys. I saw this unfairness on a daily basis with my brothers — particularly Samuel and Jared — getting far more freedom to do what they wanted to do than Clarinda and I had. Watching them grow up, I knew they were going to find life just generally easier for them than it was for us women.

As Clarinda’s marriage fell apart and she attempted to end it, I saw her struggles and understood how desperate she was. I talked to my father and to Baker, my husband, to try to figure out how I could help Clarinda. But the laws were never on her side. I was afraid she might do something rash — and I kept trying to tell her that she must not do anything to harm James. I was hoping, somehow, that I could help her find a way to end her marriage yet keep her children. No matter what I did, however, her situation just got worse with every passing day. Ultimately, her decision to murder James was hers alone, but I felt guilty about it, believing that perhaps I might have done something to make her believe that she had no other option. Attending her trial was one of the most difficult things I have ever done and I knew that she would probably not avoid prison time.

After her conviction, living in West Turin became almost impossible. But I remained at first, hoping that I might be able to help with an appeal. During that time, I was unable to successfully carry a child to full term, and I lost a boy, Cassius, in 1862, just two years after Clarinda’s death. Before I convinced Baker to leave West Turin, I gave birth to two beautiful daughters: Julia Harriet and Bessie. Once I had convinced Baker that we had to leave, I felt tremendous relief that I no longer had to endure the stares and innuendoes that I experienced every time I went to town to buy something.

Like Clarinda, I didn’t want to remain married to Baker, but I was determined to wait until the right moment. As laws began to change, I knew my chance at divorce was coming closer every single day. And it finally came. After our divorce, Sarah Etta headed for Kansas City to try to find a life for herself — she was never going to end up like her Aunt Clarinda — and to help out with the family’s finances.

Unfortunately, although laws had improved for women, they had not changed a great deal. Deciding to work as a fancy lady and then to own her own establishment was genius on Sarah Etta’s part. If she had not fallen in love and found herself pregnant, perhaps her life would have been quite different. But I have learned that there is no point in crying over spilled milk — what will be will be. Sarah Etta did a remarkable job of taking care of herself and helping out her family as well. But she never got over the loss of her baby’s father and the fact that she couldn’t have Gracie with her in Kansas City.

Since her death, Julia and I have tried hard to make Gracie’s life not just “good” but we wanted her to have a chance to do something with her life. After Sarah Etta’s death and after we had settled the messy will, Julia and I concentrated on Gracie. We made sure that she will finish school and we hope that she is going to become a nurse; that is what she says she is interested in.

Several years ago, I met a man named John Kell. When I met him, he was still married to someone else, but his wife died in 1891. We were married on 10 November 1892. This has not been the same marriage I had with Baker. First of all, we are beyond worrying or thinking about having children. I am glad that part of my life is over. John and I are “equal” in all ways. We keep our finances separated; we both support ourselves. We enjoy doing things together — something that Baker and I rarely did. I don’t know how many years I have left, but marriage to John was a good decision.

So on my 62nd birthday, it is easy to look back and see the good things — and the pain of loss. I would have wished that my beautiful Sarah Etta and Bessie would have lived longer, but I still have Julia and Effie.
